title: Black Blade and preventive measures for birds (Spanish wind industry)
abstract: The impact of wind turbines on birdlife is a major concern within the wind sector. For this reason, during the design and processing phases of wind farms, exhaustive environmental impact studies are carried out, including full-cycle bird studies, to minimise the effects on local bird and bat species. In addition, the sector is constantly looking for solutions to further reduce the effects that wind turbines can have on birds. Among the solutions analyzed is the integration of passive visual signals that increase the visibility of wind farms for birds and allow them to take evasive actions in time. In 2020, the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research (NINA) published a study analysing the effect of painting one of the three blades of the wind turbine in a contrasting colour as a strategy to increase the visibility of the rotor in motion1 . The report states that painting one of the blades on 4 wind turbines at the Norwegian Smøla wind farm black resulted in a 70% reduction in mortality for certain native bird species, compared to adjacent wind turbines. While this is a promising result, it is only a pilot project developed in a very specific habitat. The article itself concludes that more studies are needed to confirm whether the results obtained under these conditions and for certain bird species can be extrapolated to other scenarios. This is due to the fact that the study was carried out on small wind turbines (2.1-2.3 MW of power and a hub height of 70 m), in a specific terrestrial location, and with a very particular contrasting color (black on a snowy environment). In addition, the project was carried out in a region where lowmedium temperatures (around 16oC) are recorded, and the studies did not consider the effects that high temperatures and high levels of solar radiation could have on the color of the blades proposed. ## Spanish Document translated from

**AEE-Implicaciones-del-Pintado-de-Palas-de-Negro-v2022.pdf (aeeolica.org)**

## **“ Implications of Painting black blades: preventive measures for birds”**

The impact of wind turbines on birdlife is a major concern within the wind sector. For this reason, during the design and processing phases of wind farms, exhaustive environmental impact studies are carried out, including full-cycle bird studies, to minimise the effects on local bird and bat species. In addition, the sector is constantly looking for solutions to further reduce the effects that wind turbines can have on birds. Among the solutions analyzed is the integration of passive visual signals that increase the visibility of wind farms for birds and allow them to take evasive actions in time. In 2020, the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research (NINA) published a study analysing the effect of painting one of the three blades of the wind turbine in a contrasting colour as a strategy to increase the visibility of the rotor in motion1 . The report states that painting one of the blades on 4 wind turbines at the Norwegian Smøla wind farm black resulted in a 70% reduction in mortality for certain native bird species, compared to adjacent wind turbines. While this is a promising result, it is only a pilot project developed in a very specific habitat. The article itself concludes that more studies are needed to confirm whether the results obtained under these conditions and for certain bird species can be extrapolated to other scenarios. This is due to the fact that the study was carried out on small wind turbines (2.1-2.3 MW of power and a hub height of 70 m), in a specific terrestrial location, and with a very particular contrasting color (black on a snowy environment). In addition, the project was carried out in a region where lowmedium temperatures (around 16oC) are recorded, and the studies did not consider the effects that high temperatures and high levels of solar radiation could have on the color of the blades proposed. In the same way, and as stated in a report by AWWI (American Wind Wildlife Institute) where the Norwegian study is analyzed, the small number of fatalities reported both before and after applying the treatment to the blades, limits the validity of the conclusions that can be drawn from the effect of black paint: a reduction or increase of a couple of collisions has a significant impact on the results2 . During 2020, some information appeared in the press about pilot projects developed in Spanish wind farms, consisting of painting the blades and vinyl of the towers with eyes to protect birds (Figure 1)

As a result of these experimental projects, in the Environmental Impact Assessments of new wind farms, some Administrations have begun to require as a compensatory measure the painting of 2/3 of one of the blades in black for all new wind turbines. This Association considers that the requirement of these measures is not the most appropriate, because the painting of the blades in black could have negative technical implications on the behavior of the wind turbines, and, to date, they have only been applied in pilot projects. The reports themselves warn of the limitations of the studies

and the need to carry out new research to confirm the results in other locations. In addition, before demanding specific measures, AEE considers that other alternatives that could equal or improve these benefits should be analyzed, together with the sector.

Technically, any colour can be applied to wind turbine blades, but there are very justified reasons for the industry to choose colours such as light grey (RAL 7035) or offwhite colours, such as RAL 9018 (papyrus white) or RAL 9010 (pure white). Painting 2/3 of a racket black poses several technical, legal, environmental and commercial problems, which are discussed below. 1. TECHNICAL IMPLICATIONS There are several technical implications as a result of painting a blade black, since black paint has different material properties than gray or white paints. The main negative repercussions are: 1. Black paint is generally a weaker and less impact-resistant paint, which causes accelerated wear and cracking phenomena. 2. The black paint means that the blades are overheated on sunny days. Solar radiation in summer will cause a considerable increase in the temperature of the black blade, with a significant increase in the thermal stresses supported by the blade being expected. This excessive heating will negatively influence its useful life and can cause the delamination of the structure, ultimately leading to the failure of the blade. Studies carried out by manufacturers show that black blades reach temperatures that can cause the failure of the structure (resins and adhesives). These results, which have been validated in tests on blades, are consistent with the experience of paint manufacturers, showing that blades with black paints can reach temperatures 17oC higher than those achieved by grey/white paints. The studies carried out by manufacturers are detailed in the Annex. 3. Black paint has different conductive properties than greyish or white paints, which can negatively influence the lightning protection system of wind turbine blades. 4. When painting a blade black, its accessories must also be painted, such as vortex generators, Gurney fins, lightning receivers, winglets or serrated edges, etc. Pigments and other additives can affect the strength and functionality of these components. 5. The additional weight of the black paint on the blade can lead to higher fatigue stresses that reduce its useful life and affect the economic performance of the assets. For these reasons, changing the blade design by painting it black can have an impact on the depreciation and technical performance of the blade, potentially reducing the energy production of the wind turbine due to premature wear and cracking, or by excess protective materials to be added.

The colors of the blades must comply with a series of national and international regulations on aeronautical easements. In Spain, the Guide for Signalling and Lighting of Turbines and Wind Farms4 , approved by the State Aviation Safety Agency (AESA), defines the specifications that wind turbines must comply with, which, due to their height, can be considered obstacles to air traffic. In this guide, EASA points out that, in order to ensure the safety and regularity of aircraft operations, wind turbine blades must be painted white or greyish. A color change should be coordinated with applicable easement regulations.

5.2.1 Signage As a general rule, for wind farm signage, the rotor blades, the nacelle and the upper 2/3 of the support mast of all wind turbines shall be painted entirely white or greyish, the chromaticity of which shall be within the limits established in Royal Decree 862/2009, of 14 May.  Technical Standards for the Design and Operation of Aerodromes ‐ for Public Use, Appendix 1; Figure A1 2 Colors of aeronautical surface lights. The promoter of the new installation can determine, with adequate justification, the suitability of another type of signage due to the environment of the site, such as wind farms located in areas where there is snow for a large part of the year (Figure 5.2.). If another type of signage is chosen, it must guarantee an equivalent level of security and be accepted by EASA (Image 5.1.). 5.2.2 Colours The signs will be, as a general rule, traffic white (RAL 9016) and traffic orange (RAL 2009). Alternatively, the traffic red colour (RAL 3020) will be allowed in the case of wind turbines together with greyish white (RAL 9002), agate grey (RAL 7038) or light grey (RAL 7035). Alternatively, traffic red (RAL 3020) will be permitted together with greyish white (RAL 9002), agate grey (RAL 7038) or light grey (RAL 7035). The use of the relevant daytime light colours is permitted. European aviation safety legislation establishes that the components of wind turbines installed at sea must be painted in white. In other neighbouring European countries, it is required to apply red stripes or dots on the blades as a measure to guarantee air safety, a requirement that is not easily combined with the painting of the 4 AESA (2017), Guide to Signalling and Lighting of Turbines and Wind Farms.

Black blades. This is a problem for blade manufacturers, who need to standardize product specifications as much as possible in order to produce blades with similar characteristics, reduce complexity in their production chain and maintain competitiveness. Finally, it is necessary to bear in mind that in order to be marketed, all wind turbine models must go through an exhaustive testing and certification process. Wind turbine paint systems are intrinsically embedded in the turbine type certification. Manufacturers invest a lot of effort in developing the best paint systems, and it is not an easy task to recertify a different paint system.

From the manufacturer's perspective, painting a black blade requires additional investment in blade painting equipment, as it is not possible to mix the paint lines to prevent the colors from mixing. Also, since the blades are manufactured in batches of three, introducing a black blade increases the logistical complexity of the process, in handling, transport to the wind farm and installation. From a maintenance perspective, blade inspections are typically performed with cameras and drones. It is expected that the inspection of black blades will be more difficult than those of lighter colors, complicating the detection of cracks and other possible critical defects. In the same way, since the accessories of the black blade must be the same color, the inventory needs of maintenance companies increase, while adding complexity to logistics and the supply chain.

4. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPLICATIONS As mentioned in the introduction, the study carried out at the Smøla wind farm (Norway) has several limitations.

1. 4 blades painted black were tested, obtaining a decrease in bird mortality in the 4 marked wind turbines compared to the 4 wind turbines adjacent to them. This means that the results must be treated with care due to the limited number of machines studied, as the study itself concludes.

2. The study verified the reduction in mortality of the willow partridge (Lagopus Lagopus or "Moerassneeuwhoen"), without being able to evaluate the effect it has had on other species of local avifauna.

3. The low mortality reported, both before and after applying the paint to the blades, limits the conclusions that can be drawn from the effect of the black paint.

4. The site conditions are very specific, given that the study has been carried out by painting a white or greyish wind turbine blade black in a snowy terrestrial environment. This means that wind turbines can gain visibility through a black blade and/or especially through black stripes on the tower. In fact, it is hypothesized that the black stripes on the wind turbine tower would have a greater effect.

5. The study is based on the NREL report, where, firstly, it is concluded that black was not the most effective colour, preferring others such as blue, green and, above all, red and yellow5 . Black is recommended as it is understood as the most economical color. However, this conclusion applied only to the case of blades with a neutral white background. By carrying out the study with a colorful background, using images of California where yellow and brown colors predominate on a blue sky, similar to those found in the Spanish landscape, different results were obtained: it was concluded that the results varied according to the color of the landscape, considerably increasing the visibility of the unpainted blades on this type of background. In other words, in this case, the results show that there are no significant differences between using an unpainted and a painted blade, and that the most visible colors were blue and green. Black and red obtained similar results. Therefore, larger studies are required to corroborate the effectiveness of these measures.

One of the projects being carried out will be located in the Netherlands, where 7 turbines of the Eemshaven wind farm will have a blade painted black to investigate their effect on birdlife6 . However, small wind turbines have been installed on land in this farm, so complementary studies will be required in the future. In other words, before generalizing the practice of blade painting, it is necessary to ensure that it is effective, also testing other configurations that can mitigate the technical, legal and commercial implications. Finally, one of the biggest problems facing wind power is the visual impact of wind turbines. To mitigate this impact, numerous studies have been carried out with the aim of finding the most neutral colours, one of the reasons why wind turbine blades and towers are painted greyish or white. Painting a blade black would increase the visual impact of the parks, increasing local rejection of them.

The hypothesis of applying a contrast paint to a wind turbine blade seeks to reduce the blur due to rotor movement, which reduces bird collision. However, other typologies and colors other than black can also be valid to achieve this goal. The Wind Energy Business Association proposes alternative typologies and colours, which would achieve the objective of achieving a contrast between the wind turbines and the landscape by increasing their visibility, without the visual impact being excessively increased. The examples of proposed typologies are shown in Figure 2.

Includes the blade with the tip of another color; and the painting of two or three stripes of different sizes. Figure 2: Alternative proposals to increase the visibility of the blades for birdlife. The colours proposed as an alternative to black are traffic red (RAL 3020) and traffic orange (RAL 2009), as shown in Figure 3.

Figure 3: Alternative color proposal

It is important to take into account the ambient temperature of the wind farm for this choice.

Other benefits of these options are that they are already included in manufacturers' catalogs and could be started without the need for prior certifications. In addition, they are in accordance with the designs required by aeronautical bodies for the signalling of aircraft obstacles.

4 CONCLUSIONS The painting of blades in black entails various unknown effects on wind turbines and interferes with the current regulation on aeronautical easements. In addition, the benefits of these measures are not scientifically proven or validated. For all these reasons, this Association requests the following

1. Eliminate the requirement to paint 2/3 of one of the wind turbine blades black as a compensatory measure for the environmental impact assessment processes of new wind farms.

2. To advance in the analysis of alternative solutions, which contribute to reducing the impact of wind farms on birdlife, without affecting the performance and technical characteristics of wind turbines.

3. Take advantage of the different financing mechanisms available within the framework of the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (RTRP), such as the measures included in the PERTE for Renewable Energies, Hydrogen and Storage.

4. Align any additional requirements with aviation safety legislation and EASA

## ANNEX I. VALIDATION PLAN CARRIED OUT BY BLADE MANUFACTURERS.

In order to check the technical feasibility of painting the blades black, the blade manufacturers have carried out a validation plan consisting of a series of studies and tests. In particular, they wanted to check the temperatures that the black blade would reach when exposed to solar radiation. It was concluded that the black paint posed a risk to the blades since they could reach temperatures above 70oC due to solar radiation and ambient temperatures. The tests carried out are described below.

1. ACCELERATED HEAT TRANSFER TEST First, an accelerated heat transfer test was carried out in a technology centre, "Study of surface temperature under simulated solar radiation". This test was carried out in accordance with the UNE EN ISO 12543-4:2011 standard "Glass for building. Laminated glass and laminated safety glass. Part 4: Durability test methods.", and under the following conditions: • Simulated solar radiation: 900±100 W/m2 . IEC 61400 sets a value of 1,000 W/m2. • Initial ambient temperature of the test chamber: 25oC • Ambient temperature reached during the test: 37oC • Duration of the test: 1 hour from the time a temperature stabilization is achieved. Figure 4 shows the arrangement of the panels and temperature sensors used: T1 and T2 correspond to the sample painted black (RAL 9004); T3 and T4 to the grey sample (RAL 7035); and T9 at room temperature. It is shown schematically in Figure 5.

The results obtained are shown in Figure 6 and Table 1. It is found that the temperatures reached in the black painted blade (71.3oC on average) are significantly higher than in the grey sample (59.5oC on average), for an ambient temperature of 37.7oC. In other words, a difference of 11oC is obtained between the average temperatures reached between the samples of both colors. In addition, a difference of 13oC is observed in maximum temperatures.

Table 1: Results of the study of surface temperature under simulated solar radiation

- Average maximum temperature of the test location: 27oC. • Test location: Navarre. • Thermocouple monitoring. • Duration: one month.

In view of these results, and taking into account that the glass transition temperature (Tg) is 72oC for the epoxy resin of the composite material and 65oC for the adhesive, painting the blades black would pose a great risk of affecting the mechanical properties of the critical materials of the blades due to the temperatures that can be reached on their surface. The glass transition temperature is the temperature at which the epoxy resin or adhesive changes from a glassy (solid) state to a soft, rubbery state. It can be considered the point at which there is an appreciable reduction in physical properties, resulting from exposure to high temperatures7 .

In other words, the accelerated laboratory test shows that in the blades painted black, temperatures close to or higher than the critical temperatures of their structural materials (resin and adhesives) would be reached. Therefore, manufacturers cannot technically recommend the use of black paint on the blades as it implies a high probability of structural failure of the blade at these critical temperatures.

2. NATURAL AGEING ASSAY As the next step in the validation plan, a natural ageing assay was carried out to corroborate the above conclusions. In it, two real blade sections, one painted in black (RAL 9004) and the other used as a reference painted in grey (RAL 7035), are exposed to natural solar radiation. As conditions of the test: • Angle of incidence: 15o-30o and south orientation.

Both sections were instrumented with 8 thermocouples, as shown in Figure 8. Three of them were located on the surface of the blade (P2, P3 and P9), and another 5 on the inside (P6 on the adhesive, P4 and P8 on the spars, and P5 and P7 on the resin).

Figure 8: Paddle section painted black with 8 thermocouples. Temperature data were monitored and collected every 10 minutes during the month of June. The maximum values collected in both sections are shown in Table 2.

Figure 9 exemplifies the evolution of temperatures in both sections of blades (N for the sensors of the black blade, and G for those of the paddle painted gray) on the hottest days of the month.

Table 2: Maximum temperature measured in each section of the blade on the surface of the blade (P2, P3 and P9) and inside it (P4, P5, P6, P7 and P8

The results obtained corroborate the conclusions reached in the "study of surface temperature under simulated solar radiation" detailed in the previous section. In the black painted racket, temperatures of up to 90oC are reached, with differences of up to 17oC compared to the gray racket. In addition, the most critical temperatures are reached in areas with adhesive or resin, where the glass transition temperatures (Tg) of the materials are close to or exceeded.

3. EXPERIENCE OF PAINT MANUFACTURERS Finally, based on the experience of blade manufacturers, the temperature reached in service on the surface of blades painted in white or grey (RAL 7035 or RAL 9018) is between 40-50oC. Paint manufacturers, based on their internal laboratory tests and experience, establish that black paint reaches temperatures 30-40oC higher than those reached by gray and white paints. Studies that had been carried out on the temperatures reached by a painting according to its colour concluded that, on a sunny day with little wind and an ambient temperature of 33oC, a surface painted black can reach 90oC, as can be seen in Figure 10.

Figure 10: Comparison of temperatures reached according to the color of the paint applied on a sunny day with an ambient temperature of 33oC (90oF), where black paint is observed reaching 90oC (190oF) (Source: Pockett, 2010). A Review of Heat-Reflective Paints

Taking into account the results of the experiments carried out, it can be concluded that there is structural risk in blades painted black in hot climates, as is the case in Spain. **Therefore, the use of the color black on wind turbine blades is not recommended.**

17 The most temperature-sensitive structural materials of the blade are resin (Tg=72oC) and adhesive (Tg=65oC). The temperatures obtained during both tests were close to, and even exceeded, the critical temperatures of these materials, so their mechanical properties would be affected, negatively influencing their useful life and ultimately leading to the failure of the blade.
